extracted.intended_audience: environmental and administrative law practitioners, state regulators, agency counsel, and regulated parties
extracted.subtask_description: Standards for how federal agencies must handle and respond to public comments during APA notice-and-comment rulemaking, as clarified by the Supreme Court in Ohio v. EPA. Includes what counts as a sufficient response, comment specificity, and related procedural considerations (e.g., stays).

rubrics_metrics.name: Final rule must consider comments and offer a satisfactory explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the APA, publication of a proposed rule triggers an opportunity for public comment; after the comment period the agency must decide whether to continue, modify, or withdraw its proposed rule, and the final rule must consider the comments and offer a satisfactory explanation for its action and may not ignore problems raised during the public comment period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a foundational APA requirement: agencies cannot adopt final rules that ignore substantive issues raised in comments. Courts may set aside rules that fail to show they considered and responded to comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency must provide a reasoned response to commenters' substantive concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: When commenters raise concerns about an agency’s methodology, assumptions, or reasoning of a proposed action, the agency must provide a reasoned response to those comments; failure to do so can render the final rule unlawful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from Ohio v. EPA: commenters worried that the FIP’s effectiveness depended on 100% state participation; the Court held EPA offered no reasoned response explaining why fewer participants would not undermine the FIP’s purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgment of concern is not a substitute for explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Awareness of commenters’ concerns does not satisfy the obligation to respond; an agency cannot merely acknowledge or 'sidestep' an issue and must explain why the concern does not change the agency’s decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court rejected EPA’s argument that a broad severability provision constituted a reasoned response, noting the provision 'did not address the [Petitioners'] concern so much as sidestep it.' Agencies must address the substance of the concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanations must appear in the final rule (the record for review)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the agency has an explanation for why a concern does not affect its decision, that explanation must appear in the final rule (or the administrative record) rather than being absent or only implied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion observed that 'if there [was] an explanation, it does not appear in the final rule,' which undercuts the agency’s position on review; courts look to the final rule/record to determine whether a reasoned explanation exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable specificity requirement for comments: notice, not verbatim rehearsal
rubrics_metrics.description: A commenter is not required to 'rehearse the identical argument made before the agency' during the comment period; rather, the reasonable specificity rule requires that a comment give the agency notice of the substance of the challenge so it has a chance to consider it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard balances allowing judicial review with ensuring agencies received notice. The Court found Petitioners sufficiently put EPA on notice even without repeating an identical legal formulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: No requirement to return to the agency before seeking judicial relief for matters already raised
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters are not required to file a motion asking the agency to reconsider a final rule before seeking judicial relief if the concern was already raised during the comment period and the agency had a chance to address it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court rejected EPA’s argument that petitioners should have sought agency reconsideration, stating 'nothing requires [commenters] to return to EPA to raise (again) a concern EPA already had a chance to address.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Court will consider stay requests using four traditional factors
rubrics_metrics.description: When deciding whether to stay an agency action pending judicial review, courts weigh: (1) likelihood of success on the merits; (2) whether the applicant will suffer irreparable harm; (3) whether a stay will substantially injure the other party; and (4) where the public interest lies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Ohio v. EPA the Supreme Court’s majority focused primarily on the likelihood of success (whether the FIP was 'reasonable and reasonably explained') when granting a stay; litigants should prepare arguments on all four factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency cannot impose a blanket plan based on unwarranted assumptions without addressing comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an agency’s proposed rule relies on key assumptions (e.g., full participation by affected jurisdictions), the agency must address comments challenging those assumptions and explain how outcomes would differ if assumptions fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the FIP case, EPA assumed all 23 noncompliant states would participate; commenters questioned results if fewer states participated and argued EPA would need new assessment and modeling. The agency’s failure to explain the assumption’s consequences was central to the Court’s finding of inadequate explanation.
